headline: Armed man patrolling next to elementary school tests Montana’s gun tolerance
author: Annie Gowen

paragraphs.text: The years-long standoff between a gun-wielding man and an elementary school in Billings, Montana, began as a mundane dispute between neighbors — a broken tool, motor oil spilled in the horseradish bed.

It quickly escalated into threats and a restraining order. Eventually one of the neighbors, Gabriel Metcalf, began patrolling his property daily with his gun, directly across the street from Broadwater Elementary School.

He was arrested in 2023 for unlawful possession of a firearm in a school zone. But a federal court overturned his conviction last year, ruling that Montana’s gun laws permitted him to do what he did. He resumed his patrols this September.

Parents and school officials say they are horrified by the sight of Metcalf pacing with a 20-gauge shotgun in front of the home he shares with his mother. They say they are terrified Metcalf could just break down and open fire one day.

To protect students, school administrators have changed the way children walk to school, curtailed recess and hung a huge black tarp over the playground fence. They’re now hoping their legislators can find a solution.

The conflict has tested the limits of Montana’s 2021 law to allow permit-less carry and set off a debate over school safety and fiercely held gun rights in a conservative state where independence and self-reliance are prized.
Tanya Ludwig, a member of the Billings school board who attended the school as a child, wept at a recent meeting.
“This guy could go off and shoot someone,” she said through tears. “I don’t want to have a parent bury a child. It’s not an easy thing to go through. We need to get this addressed.”
Metcalf declined an interview request.

His mother, Vivian Young, says her son is simply trying to keep her safe from a former neighbor who threatened her but has since moved away. She says the family is being victimized by overzealous meddlers, whom she referred to as “Karens.” Her son is just exercising his Second Amendment rights, she said.

“The angry mob is doing everything they can do to harass us,” she said. “All this town needs is a good sale on pitchforks and tiki torches. We would have had them on our lawn. It is so out of control.”
On Nov. 16, the school board voted to allow parents to start fundraising to build a wall around the school to permanently end the view of Metcalf and his patrols. The expected cost is $475,000.
“It’s ridiculous,” Young said. “This is Montana. Everybody’s armed.”

Young, 74, runs a small at-home tailoring business, and Metcalf, 52, lives in a small trailer on the property on Broadwater Avenue. He began patrolling the parcel in 2023 because of the unnerving actions of their neighbor at the time, Young said.

The man began coming over without invitation and doing things like dumping motor oil in her horseradish bed and spraying her bee house with wasp repellent, she said. “He would do these random things — odd, bizarre,” she said.
His behavior soon morphed into violent threats — to kill Young’s pet rabbit and eventually Young herself. She obtained a restraining order against him in 2022.
Metcalf’s near-daily checks on his home’s perimeter raised immediate alarms among parents at the school.

In August 2023, Metcalf was arrested and charged with unlawful possession of a firearm in a school zone under the federal government’s 1990 Gun-Free School Zones Act, which prohibits unauthorized individuals from possessing a firearm within 1,000 feet of a school. He eventually pleaded guilty and received three years of probation.
But in September 2025, a three-judge panel on the San Francisco-based U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit overturned his conviction by a 2-1 vote.

Metcalf’s lawyers had argued that Montana’s 2021 permit-less carry law — one of 29 across the country — meant Metcalf was legally authorized to possess a firearm as part of the school zone law’s exemptions, which allow “state-licensed individuals” to have firearms near schools. In his opinion, U.S. Circuit Judge Lawrence VanDyke, deemed this argument “plausible.”
VanDyke also wrote that Young’s neighbor had “stalked and threatened Metcalf and his mother” and repeatedly violated the protection order.

“I think this case illustrates the really difficult tension between restrictive federal laws and permissive state laws,” said Joseph Blocher, a law professor at Duke University, who is the director of the school’s Center for Firearms Law. “This is the kind of challenge that arises when states are loosening their gun laws while the federal government is trying to enforce nationwide rules.”
Metcalf resumed his patrols this fall, his mother said, because the family had received death threats over the ongoing drama, as well as an unrelated attempted break-in.

Billings Public Schools Superintendent Erwin Garcia told the board of trustees in September that he drove by the house and saw Metcalf dressed in a face mask and a hoodie toting what he called a “high-caliber weapon.” Young told The Washington Post the weapon was a shotgun.
“It was completely unacceptable,” Garcia said. “This is the time when kids are supposed to be going to school. We’re talking 7:20 or 7:30.”
“But federal judges gave this person his freedom,” the superintendent added. “He’s not doing anything illegal.”
Emergency meetings ensued. The tarp shielding the playground — first added to the fence in 2023 — went back up. Parents began asking to withdraw their kids from the school.
Sgt. Jeff Stovall, spokesman for the Billings Police Department, said the department has increased patrols by school resource officers and others but feels it has few other options to ensure safety.
“We’re at the mercy of the court because precedent has been set,” Stovall said. “Unless there’s an actual crime and probable cause to arrest somebody.”
At the September board meeting, Garcia wondered from the dais if another option might be shutting down the school altogether and somehow finding a place for its 380 students.
“Is this the Montana way?” he asked aloud.

James Reavis, the Democratic state representative who represents the area, said he would propose legislation to address the gun loophole in the next session in January — perhaps by amending the state’s disorderly conduct laws.
“I’m confident we can come up with a bipartisan solution,” he said.
But that feels like an eternity to the parents with children at Broadwater Elementary School.
Katie Brand, a mother of two who lives nearby, told the board in September that she wept with staff when Metcalf reemerged.

“Legislation … feels really impossible at this point and so far down the road,” she said, saying she was concerned about her children’s safety — and her own. “This could be happening to anyone in this city and happen to anyone in this state.”

The parents provided a statement saying that their “priority is ensuring a safe environment for our children to learn and play” and that fundraising efforts are “focused on long-term safety improvements.”
Young said she and her son remain unbowed.
“It has nothing to do with the school,” she said. “People need to resolve to the fact that we have a right to be armed. This is government tyranny.”
Razzan Nakhlawi contributed to this report.
